tr.td: 'O 'ntufato, "the angry one"; the Corriere della Sera headlined him "Faccia feroce" (fierce face)
Nola and Saviano, east of Naples, Italy
Head of a Camorra clan that grew into the most powerful alliance in Campania in the 1980s
11 September 1992, in a hideout near Naples, after about ten years as a fugitive
Became a state witness in 1993 to 1994 and named politicians, among them a former interior minister
Raffaele Cutolo and his Nuova Camorra Organizzata
Nuova Famiglia, formed between 1979 and 1981 with the Nuvoletta and Bardellino groups, according to a parliamentary anti-mafia report

content.p: For about ten years the most wanted man in Campania lived underground, and the Camorra grew around him. Carmine Alfieri, known as 'o 'ntufato, "the angry one", was captured by the carabinieri at dawn on 11 September 1992, asleep in a hole dug beneath a country house near Naples. He was 48. His bodyguards, according to the Spanish newspaper El País, carried no weapons, and neither did he.

Over the next two years the man who had run the pyramid of Neapolitan clans that investigators credited him with building did something that shook Italian politics. He agreed to talk to prosecutors. By March 1994 la Repubblica was reporting that he had begun to cooperate, and the accusations that followed reached the Christian Democratic Party and a former interior minister. The sections below follow how a boy from the countryside around Nola became that kind of boss, what the authorities said he did, and what his decision to talk set in motion. Much of the account rests on the claims of prosecutors, police and other former mobsters, and where a claim was never tested in court, the text says so.
content.h2: An oath over a dead father
content.p: The legend the press repeated begins with a vow. The Corriere della Sera wrote in April 1993 that Alfieri swore a blood oath at the age of ten, kneeling over the body of his father, killed in what the paper called a rustic duel in the country around Nola. A clan profile published by Napolionline gives a different age and a slightly different story: the oath was sworn in 1953, when Carmine was seven, together with his brother Salvatore, to avenge their father Antonio, who had died in a feud between rival gangs. The two accounts disagree on the age and on whether the killing was a duel or a gang feud.

Both agree that the first revenge was taken by the brother. Napolionline says that three years later Salvatore killed the man who had killed their father, a man named Tore Notaio, at the social club in Saviano, and that Salvatore was himself later executed in a restaurant in Pompei. Carmine, the Corriere wrote, was by then locked into a spiral of violence that showed even in his face, which is how he earned the nickname 'o 'ntufato for his grim and menacing expression.

The Corriere's profile then lists what it called the inevitable steps in a camorrista's career. Alfieri was first arrested while still a youth, walking around with a 9-calibre pistol at his belt. After he got out, the paper wrote, his record filled with frauds, robberies, extortion, bombings, drug trafficking and murders. It added one massacre, at Torre Annunziata, for which he avoided conviction.

In the late 1970s Raffaele Cutolo and his Nuova Camorra Organizzata were the force to beat in Campania. According to the parliamentary anti-mafia commission's report on the Camorra, Cutolo's rise was itself a reaction to the weight of Sicilian Cosa Nostra in the tobacco smuggling trade. Between 1979 and 1981, the report says, a confederation called the Nuova Famiglia took shape, led by the Nuvoletta and Bardellino groups and Alfieri, with the aim of destroying Cutolo's organisation before it could win a monopoly of criminal power in the region. The commission described the Nuvoletta and Bardellino leaders as men of honour with links to Cosa Nostra.

The commission also records a round of talks in 1981 on a Bardellino estate at Vallesana. Cutolo, who had been rearrested after an escape, could not attend and was represented by his brother Pasquale and his right-hand man Vincenzo Casillo, among others. Across the table sat Bardellino, Alfieri and Pasquale Galasso. According to Galasso, as the report relays it, the meetings produced nothing, partly because Nuvoletta was playing a double game and trying to pose as an arbitrator. Killings followed one after another, and the brothers of both Alfieri and Galasso were killed by Cutolo's gangs.

The year 1982 was the bloodiest in Campania, with 284 murders, the commission says, and the same year marked the start of Cutolo's decline and Alfieri's rise. The report links the turning of the tide to the kidnapping of Ciro Cirillo, a regional politician seized by the Red Brigades in 1981, and to the negotiations for his release. Galasso's version, as la Repubblica summarised it in 1994, was that Antonio Gava and the Christian Democrats wanted Cirillo freed at any price and first approached Alfieri, who refused to be used by politicians. Cutolo stepped in instead and gained standing when Cirillo came home. Galasso added that Gava and his son, in his telling, were then pressed by Cutolo to honour agreements and threatened with a scandal. These are the words of a former mobster, reported by a newspaper, and not findings of a court.

Repubblica also reported that Alfieri told prosecutors about the killing of Vincenzo Casillo, Cutolo's right hand, in Rome, which the paper dated to 1982. According to the judges quoted in the article, that murder sealed an alliance between the Alfieri clan and the leadership of the Christian Democrats.

The episode most often tied to Alfieri's name is a shooting in the coastal town of Torre Annunziata. It came as the winners of the war against Cutolo fell out among themselves. According to the parliamentary report, the Nuvoletta and Gionta groups stood on one side and Bardellino, Alfieri and Fabbrocino on the other. Ciro Nuvoletta had been shot dead on 10 June 1984 at the Vallesana estate where the earlier talks had been held, by armed men from the Alfieri, Galasso and Bardellino groups, the report says.

On Sunday 26 August a commando of at least 14 people arrived by bus and two cars outside the Fishermen's Club, where members of the Gionta clan gathered. The report says the group stepped out and opened fire, killing seven Gionta men and wounding seven. Other publications gave other counts. El País, writing in 1992, put the number of attackers at about 15 and the dead at eight, and the Corriere and la Repubblica also spoke of eight dead. The commission explained why the attack mattered: to drive into the home town of the Gionta boss, shoot into the crowd and leave unharmed was to show that he could not protect himself or his people.

Whether Alfieri ordered it is where the sources differ most. Napolionline names him as the man who commissioned the attack. El País wrote that police held him responsible but had not been able to prove a link to the shooting. In 1994 la Repubblica noted that he had come out of the trial unscathed, and the Corriere said he had avoided conviction. Alfieri stands in the record as a man blamed for the massacre by investigators and never convicted of it.

After Torre Annunziata, the commission says, the Alfieri clan emerged gradually as the strongest, wiping out what was left of Cutolo's network and fighting a harsher war against the Nuvoletta clan and its allies. Between 1984 and 1989 an organisation that had traditionally worked around Nola spread across the province of Naples: toward Pomigliano d'Arco, the Nocera and Sarno plain, the coast between Torre Annunziata and Castellammare di Stabia, and the Vesuvius area, including Somma Vesuviana, Sant'Anastasia and Volla. The report ties that growth to new alliances, with the Galasso family of Poggiomarino, the Anastasio of Sant'Anastasia, the Moccia of Afragola, the Vangone-Limelli of Torre Annunziata and named bosses in Castellammare, Quindici, Sant'Antonio Abate and Boscoreale. In the province of Salerno it lists allies around Eboli, Battipaglia, Nocera, Angri and Scafati.

The same report says that these bosses had links with local officials and banks, and it lists arrests in the Salerno investigation of the Galasso clan, among them a former mayor of Nocera Inferiore and bank officials. That inquiry led to the arrest of Galasso himself, the commission notes.

The Corriere, in 1993, described a very different man from the sneering gunman of the legend. It said police reports portrayed a boss of notable intelligence who kept the rules, symbols and philosophical jargon of the old Camorra, and a fifty-year-old criminal entrepreneur with good international connections (translated from the Italian). When he was caught, the paper added, the hideout held books by Svevo and Goethe and records by Bach and Vivaldi. An investigator said that a man like that was no longer content to stay with his cronies and wanted to deal as an equal with the top of the state.

El País reported that Alfieri operated behind a legal front as an importer of meat and timber from Romania, building from Nola an empire that reached toward Vesuvius and the sea at Salerno. It said small-time crime had disappeared from the area because it interfered with bigger business. A report published a year earlier, it added, gave him an annual turnover of 1,5 billones de liras, in the Spanish paper's wording, more than any other Camorra or mafia organisation. The Corriere put the clan's earnings at 1,500 billion lire at least, citing Censis and Criminalpol estimates. Both were estimates, and El País itself said the figure might not be exact.

El País's report of his arrest is the fullest account. Carabinieri found him asleep in a hiding place under a rural villa, accompanied by Marzio Sepe, 38, while a second bodyguard, Vincenzo Cesarano, 31, was surprised in the apartment. The newspaper called the lack of violence all the stranger given the background. Carlo Alfiero, the colonel commanding the carabinieri in Naples, said the operation was the fruit of long and painstaking work begun many years earlier. The paper also noted that the arrest came days after that of the Sicilian mafioso Giuseppe Madonia, and judged it less significant because the Camorra carried less political and social weight than Cosa Nostra.

In April 1993 the Corriere reported that his name appeared again and again in a 199-page dossier prepared by magistrates against five prominent figures: Gava, Paolo Cirino Pomicino, Raffaele Mastrantuono, Alfredo Vito and Vincenzo Meo. The paper's source was Galasso, by then a state witness himself, who said that for at least ten years Naples had had a new viceroy, and that it was Alfieri. The paper wrote that Alfieri had eight thousand men at his disposal and, if Galasso's account was true, a circle of officials he had drawn into his court. The Corriere cautioned that the account was one man's story, saying that if it were ever proven it would be a shattering one. The dossier described Alfieri, the paper wrote, as a reference point for the clans and for business and political circles, who had offered cover and protection in exchange for similar favours. It also described a man who toasted the success of a massacre by giving the killer a Rolex.

At the start of March 1994, la Repubblica reported, Alfieri had been speaking to prosecutors for several weeks, two years after his arrest. The paper quoted him as saying that the state had beaten the Camorra and urging free bosses to cooperate. The magistrates named by the paper were Luigi Gay, Giovanni Melillo, Antonio Laudati, Paolo Mancuso and Franco Roberti, with the investigating judge Antonio Sensale. The paper said he had promised to say everything he knew, unlike bosses who were prepared only to distance themselves, and that he had told of the Cirillo affair and of dozens of crimes. It noted that after Galasso's statements eight parliamentarians and former parliamentarians stood accused of Camorra association: Gava, Cirino Pomicino, Meo, Del Mese, Patriarca and Vito of the Christian Democrats and Conte and Mastrantuono of the Socialists.

On 21 September 1994, The New York Times reported that Italian police had arrested scores of people at dawn, among them Antonio Gava, the interior minister from 1988 to 1991. He was accused of conspiring in a "perverse circuit of criminal enterprise" with Neapolitan mobsters, politicians and businessmen, and of trading favours for votes the Camorra mustered. His lawyer, Carlo Taormina, called the accusations "incomprehensible" and "incredible". The Times report quoted here does not mention Alfieri, so his part in those arrests rests on the Italian press and the trial record.

Radio Radicale holds recordings of hearings in a mass trial listed under the name of Antonio Gava and others, with Carmine Alfieri heading the list of defendants: "Alfieri + 80" before the Second Assize Court of Naples on 29 November 1995, and "Alfieri + 101" before the First Assize Court on 20 May 1997 and 1 April 1998. Hearings took place in the bunker courtrooms at Poggioreale. In the 1997 hearing the prosecutor asked the court to admit a newspaper article, a search order from Salerno prosecutors dated 13 May 1997 and a press release, in connection with Galasso's examination as a defendant.

The decision to cooperate was paid for by his family. Antonio Alfieri, the former boss's son, aged about thirty and not under the protection programme, was shot in his car in Saviano di Nola, la Repubblica reported. His girlfriend was seriously wounded. According to the paper, the young man had reportedly refused protection because he disagreed with his father's choice to turn state witness. Witnesses said two people on a large motorbike or maxi-scooter had fired.
